title: Position: Universal Aesthetic Alignment Narrows Artistic Expression
claim: A universally acclaimed masterpiece receives a low automated aesthetic score, showing that learned preference metrics misjudge valid artistic expression.
layout: Single full-bleed painting, no panels, caption carries the score comparison
description: The figure is a single image of Edvard Munch's painting The Scream (1893), reproduced full-frame with no panels, arrows, labels or overlaid text. The eye goes first to the swirling orange-red sky, then down to the skull-like figure with hands on its cheeks and an open mouth, standing on a diagonal bridge over a dark blue fjord. The palette is saturated oranges, reds and yellows against deep blues and browns, with loose, expressive brushwork. The caption, not the image, carries the argument. It says the work scored only 5.23 on the HPSv3 aesthetic reward model, while typical high-aesthetic AI images score about 10-15. This contrast shows the mismatch between metric-defined beauty and artistic value.
caption: The Scream, by Edvard Munch (1893). Despite its widely recognized artistic significance, this image only received an HPSv3 score (Ma et al., 2025) of 5.23, while typical “highaesthetic” AI-generated images can reach scores around 10 −15.
abstract: Over-aligning image generation models to a generalized aesthetic preference conflicts with user intent, particularly when "anti-aesthetic" outputs are requested for artistic or critical purposes. This adherence prioritizes developer-centered values, compromising user autonomy and aesthetic pluralism. We test this bias by constructing a wide-spectrum aesthetics dataset and evaluating state-of-the-art generation and reward models. This position paper finds that aesthetic-aligned generation models frequently default to conventionally beautiful outputs, failing to respect instructions for low-quality or negative imagery. Crucially, reward models penalize anti-aesthetic images even when they perfectly match the explicit user prompt. We confirm this systemic bias through image-to-image editing and evaluation against real abstract artworks. Our code, fine-tuned models, and datasets are available on our meta-expression intentionally anti-aesthetics webpage: https://weathon.github.io/icml2026_position/.
